title: The Three R's: Revise, Revise, Revise Education Joel
author: Joel
summary: Joel interrogates the purpose and effectiveness of after-school revision sessions in the lead-up to GCSE exams. He argues that teacher-led revision sessions often say more about teachers' anxiety than about genuine student need -- if strong teaching, regular retrieval, and knowledge-building have occurred throughout the year, extra sessions should theoretically be unnecessary. He identifies four student types: those who revise independently and attend, those for whom the session is their only revision, those who revise independently without attending, and those who do nothing at all. The argument is that most revision provision is designed for Group 2 but actually serves Group 1 students in a self-fulfilling way. Joel describes a school where after-school revision was abolished and replaced with student-led resources and open spaces, yielding greater intrinsic motivation precisely because teachers stopped doing the work for students. The core challenge: schools should build independently motivated learners, not create dependency on teacher-provided revision.
points: Revision sessions designed to fill gaps implicitly confess that teaching the curriculum was insufficient -- but the honest question is why the initial teaching did not stick, not how to cover it again faster.
The Group 2 student who relies entirely on teacher-led revision is most at risk in the exam hall: without the teacher present, the dependency the session built becomes a liability.

A department that removed after-school revision and instead maximised student access to resources found that student motivation increased -- because responsibility shifted explicitly to the student, not the teacher.
Schools risk a cynical loop: teachers run revision to feel they have done everything possible, which relieves their anxiety but does not build the intrinsic motivation students actually need.
The goal should be to make as many revision sessions as possible unnecessary by building truly self-directed, motivated learners throughout the year -- not to maximise the number of sessions offered.
quotes: What is the aim of this revision? Is it as simple as providing them with information they need to pass, or is it that they need more and more practice in order to be successful? Why do we need a teacher there at all when the students can do this themselves?

If I have taught the course, regularly retrieved knowledge throughout the curriculum, built on previous knowledge, and developed their skills, then why do I need to run a session to make sure pupils know the information? Am I just making up for some poor teaching of certain topics or am I admitting that teaching the actual course just is not enough?

The cynic in me would say many schools/teachers run revision, not for the students, but for themselves. It makes us feel better, it makes us think we have given them everything, it makes us believe that we have given them a fighting chance to achieve.

By providing a revision session for pupils, we risk the students becoming reliant on the teacher for said revision. This over reliance means that when it comes to the actual exam, and you are not there, they do not perform as well as they would have if they had completed the revision by themselves.

What we want is pupils to want to do their revision because they want to do well. There are teachers up and down the country who are doing more for their pupil's revision than the pupils are. This is surely not the ideal.

We took down as many barriers as we possibly could to ensure they could revise for themselves. They came to us, all year, and asked for resources. They found us in the corridors to ask us questions. They decided what their revision should look like.
Revision shouldn't be about how many sessions we offer, but how many sessions we make unnecessary by building truly independent, motivated learners.
